notes.front: What is Cloud Monitoring?
notes.explanation: Its services help you understand the behaviour, health and performance of your applications and of other Google Cloud services.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, “Cloud Monitoring overview”, “Cloud Monitoring overview”
notes.evidence: These services can help you to understand the behavior, health, and performance of your applications and of other Google Cloud services. Cloud Monitoring automatically collects and stores performance information for most Google Cloud services.
notes.back: A service that automatically collects and stores performance information for most Google Cloud services.
notes.example: Like the instrument panel of a car: speed, fuel and temperature for your services, gathered without you wiring each gauge.

notes.front: In Cloud Monitoring, what is a metrics scope?
notes.explanation: You can configure it to include time-series data from other Google Cloud projects and from AWS accounts.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, “Cloud Monitoring overview”, “Monitor metrics for multiple Google Cloud projects”
notes.evidence: The scoping project also hosts a metrics scope. The metrics scope defines the projects and accounts whose metrics are visible to the scoping project. You can configure the metrics scope to include time-series data from other Google Cloud projects and from AWS accounts.
notes.back: The setting, hosted by a scoping project, that defines which projects and accounts have metrics visible to that project.
notes.example: Like adding several shops' tills to one head-office screen, so one person can watch takings everywhere.

notes.front: In Cloud Monitoring, what is an uptime check?
notes.explanation: Synthetic monitors test the availability, consistency and performance of services, applications, web pages and APIs.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, “Cloud Monitoring overview”, “Proactive monitoring and validation”
notes.evidence: To test the availability, consistency, and performance of your services, applications, web pages, and APIs, create synthetic monitors. For example, you can probe HTTP, HTTPS, and TCP endpoints for responsiveness with uptime checks, and then get notified when an endpoint fails to respond.
notes.back: A synthetic monitor that probes HTTP, HTTPS or TCP endpoints for responsiveness, so you can be notified when one fails to respond.
notes.example: Like a colleague who rings your shop's phone every few minutes and tells you the moment nobody answers.

notes.front: In Cloud Monitoring, what is an alerting policy?
notes.explanation: It can monitor time-series data stored by Monitoring or logs stored by Cloud Logging.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, “Alerting overview”, “How alerting works”
notes.evidence: An alerting policy, which describes the circumstances under which you want to be alerted and how you want to be notified about an alert. The alerting policy can monitor time-series data stored by Monitoring or logs stored by Cloud Logging.
notes.back: A description of the circumstances in which you want to be alerted and how you want to be notified.
notes.example: Like a smoke alarm's settings: how much smoke sets it off, and whose phone it rings.

notes.front: In Cloud Monitoring, what is a notification channel?
notes.explanation: An alerting policy can contain one or more notification channels.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, “Alerting overview”, “How alerting works”
notes.evidence: A notification channel defines how you receive notifications when Monitoring creates an alert. For example, you can configure an alerting policy to email my-support-team@example.com and to post a Slack message to the channel #my-support-team. An alerting policy can contain one or more notification channels.
notes.back: The definition of how you receive notifications when Monitoring creates an alert, such as an email address or a Slack channel.
notes.example: Like choosing whether the alarm company phones you, texts you or emails you.

notes.front: What is Cloud Logging?
notes.explanation: It collects log data from Google Cloud resources automatically, and your applications, on-premises resources and other clouds can send it logs too.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, “Cloud Logging overview”, “Cloud Logging overview”
notes.evidence: Cloud Logging, which is a real-time log-management system with storage, search, analysis, and monitoring support. Cloud Logging automatically collects log data from Google Cloud resources. Your applications, on-premise resources, and resources from other cloud providers can send log data to Cloud Logging.
notes.back: A real-time log-management system with storage, search, analysis and monitoring support.
notes.example: Like a building's visitor book kept by a machine: every entry recorded, searchable, and able to raise the alarm.

notes.front: In Cloud Logging, what is a log sink?
notes.explanation: A sink's destination can be a project, a storage location or a service such as Pub/Sub.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, “Route log entries”, “About log sinks”
notes.evidence: When a log sink receives a log entry, it determines whether to ignore or route the log entry to the sink's destination. The log sink compares the log entry to its filters to make this decision. A sink's destination can be a project, a storage location, or a service such as Pub/Sub.
notes.back: The mechanism that routes log entries to destinations; it compares each entry with its filters to decide whether to route or ignore it.
notes.example: Like a postal sorting rule: letters matching the rule go to one address, and the rest are left alone.

notes.front: In Cloud Logging, what is the _Required bucket?
notes.explanation: Each resource has its own _Required log bucket, which receives this subset of audit logs.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, “Route log entries”, “_Required log sink”
notes.evidence: The _Required log sink in a resource routes a subset of audit logs to the resource's _Required log bucket.
notes.back: The log bucket in each resource to which the _Required log sink routes a subset of audit logs.
notes.example: Like a sealed logbook the building keeps for the inspector: certain entries always go in, and nobody can change the rule.

notes.front: In Cloud Logging, what is an aggregated sink?
notes.explanation: There are two types: intercepting and non-intercepting aggregated sinks.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, “Route log entries”, “Support for organizations and folders”
notes.evidence: You can create aggregated sinks, which route log entries for an organization or folder and their children, to the destination specified by the sink. There are two types of aggregated sinks: Non-intercepting aggregated sinks Intercepting aggregated sinks
notes.back: A sink that routes log entries for an organisation or folder and their children to the sink's destination.
notes.example: Like a head office rule that copies every branch's post to a central archive, rather than each branch setting up its own.

notes.front: What is a log-based metric?
notes.explanation: For example, one can count entries containing a particular message, or extract latency information from entries.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, “Route log entries”, “How routing log entries affects log-based metrics”
notes.evidence: Log-based metrics are Cloud Monitoring metrics that are derived from the content of log entries. For example, you can use a log-based metric to count the number of log entries that contain a particular message or to extract latency information recorded in log entries.
notes.back: A Cloud Monitoring metric derived from the content of log entries, for example a count of entries containing a particular message.
notes.example: Like counting how many times the word 'refund' appears in the complaints book each day, and graphing it.

notes.front: What is Cloud Trace?
notes.explanation: It collects latency data from Google Cloud services and instrumented applications to show how requests are processed in a microservices architecture.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, “Cloud Trace overview”, “Cloud Trace overview”
notes.evidence: Cloud Trace is a distributed tracing system for Google Cloud that tracks request latency and helps you troubleshoot performance bottlenecks across services and generative AI applications. By collecting latency data from Google Cloud services and instrumented applications, Trace helps you understand how requests are processed in a microservices architecture and identify relevant logs.
notes.back: A distributed tracing system for Google Cloud that tracks request latency and helps you troubleshoot performance bottlenecks across services.
notes.example: Like a parcel tracking page for one request: every depot it passed through, and how long it waited at each.

notes.front: What is Cloud Profiler?
notes.explanation: It attributes that information to the source code that generated it, so you can find the parts of the application using the most resources.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, “Cloud Profiler overview”, “Cloud Profiler overview”
notes.evidence: Cloud Profiler is a statistical, low-overhead profiler that continuously gathers CPU usage and memory-allocation information from your production applications. It attributes that information to the source code that generated it, helping you identify the parts of your application that are consuming the most resources,
notes.back: A statistical, low-overhead profiler that continuously gathers CPU usage and memory-allocation information from production applications.
notes.example: Like a time-and-motion study that runs all day in the live kitchen, showing which dish takes the most chef time.

notes.front: What is Error Reporting?
notes.explanation: Its central interface shows your application's top or new errors so you can fix root causes faster.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, “Error Reporting documentation”, “Error Reporting documentation”
notes.evidence: Error Reporting aggregates and displays errors produced in your running cloud services. Using the centralized error management interface, you can find your application's top or new errors so that you can fix the root causes faster.
notes.back: A service that aggregates and displays errors produced in your running cloud services.
notes.example: Like a complaints desk that groups identical complaints together and shows which ones are new today.

notes.front: What is a service level indicator (SLI)?
notes.explanation: An SLI measures performance, while a service level objective states the performance you want.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, “Concepts in service monitoring”, “Terminology”
notes.evidence: Service-level indicator (SLI): a measurement of performance. Service-level objective (SLO): a statement of desired performance.
notes.back: A measurement of performance that describes some aspect of your service.
notes.example: Like the share of trains that arrive on time: one number that measures how well the service is doing.

notes.front: What is a service level objective (SLO)?
notes.explanation: The service determines which SLIs are available, and you set SLOs based on them.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, “Concepts in service monitoring”, “Service-level objectives”
notes.evidence: An SLO is a target value for an SLI, measured over a period of time. The service determines the available SLIs, and you specify SLOs based on the SLIs. The SLO defines what qualifies as good service.
notes.back: A target value for an SLI, measured over a period of time; it defines what counts as good service.
notes.example: Like a railway promising that 95% of trains will be on time each month.

notes.front: In SLO monitoring, what does burn rate describe?
notes.explanation: Google's SLO page suggests alerting policies that warn you when this happens faster than desired.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, “Concepts in service monitoring”, “Monitoring your error budget”
notes.evidence: You can create alerting policies to warn you that your error budget is being consumed at a faster than desired rate.
notes.back: How fast the error budget is being consumed.
notes.example: Like watching how fast a monthly phone allowance is used up: half gone in two days is a warning, even though some is left.

notes.front: What is a blameless postmortem?
notes.explanation: Its purpose is to improve your technology and future, not to find who is guilty.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, “Conduct thorough postmortems”, “Conduct blameless postmortems”
notes.evidence: Effective postmortems focus on processes, tools, and technologies, and don't place blame on individuals or teams. The purpose of a postmortem analysis is to improve your technology and future, not to find who is guilty.
notes.back: A postmortem that focuses on processes, tools and technologies, and doesn't place blame on individuals or teams.
notes.example: Like an air accident report that asks why the checklist allowed the mistake, not which pilot to punish.

notes.front: What is load testing, and when does the reliability pillar suggest it during failure tests?
notes.explanation: Doing both at once replicates real-world usage during outages.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, “Perform testing for recovery from failures”, “Simulate failure scenarios”
notes.evidence: Introduce load testing alongside failure scenarios to replicate real-world usage during outages.
notes.back: Testing a system under realistic traffic load; the framework suggests introducing it alongside failure scenarios.
notes.example: Like a fire drill held on a busy day rather than an empty one, to see how the exits cope with a crowd.

notes.front: By default, which time series can you see on Cloud Monitoring pages in the console?
notes.explanation: The scoping project also stores the alerts, synthetic monitors and dashboards you configure.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, “Cloud Monitoring overview”, “Monitor metrics for multiple Google Cloud projects”
notes.evidence: By default, Cloud Monitoring pages in the Google Cloud console provide access only to the time series stored in the scoping project. The scoping project is the project that you selected with the Google Cloud console project picker. The scoping project stores the alerts, synthetic monitors, and dashboards that you configure.
notes.back: Only those stored in the scoping project, the project selected in the project picker.

notes.front: A team runs a web shop on Compute Engine virtual machines with a third-party web server. They want Cloud Monitoring to collect metrics and logs from their application and the web server. What should they install?
notes.explanation: With the Ops Agent installed on Compute Engine virtual machines, you can collect metrics and logs from your applications and third-party applications.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, “Cloud Monitoring overview”, “Cloud Monitoring overview”
notes.evidence: If you install the Ops Agent on your Compute Engine virtual machines (VMs), then you can collect metrics and logs from your applications and from third-party applications.
notes.back: The Ops Agent on the virtual machines.
notes.choices:
A) The Ops Agent on the virtual machines
B) The Cloud Profiler agent only
C) A log sink to Pub/Sub
D) An uptime check
notes.choicesExplained: The Profiler agent gathers CPU and memory profiles, not general metrics and logs. A log sink routes log entries that already reached Cloud Logging. An uptime check probes endpoints from outside; it does not collect application metrics.

notes.front: A charity wants to be told within minutes if its public donation page stops responding to web requests, whatever the cause. What should it set up in Cloud Monitoring?
notes.explanation: Uptime checks probe HTTP, HTTPS and TCP endpoints for responsiveness and notify you when an endpoint fails to respond.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, “Cloud Monitoring overview”, “Proactive monitoring and validation”
notes.evidence: For example, you can probe HTTP, HTTPS, and TCP endpoints for responsiveness with uptime checks, and then get notified when an endpoint fails to respond.
notes.back: An uptime check on the page's HTTPS endpoint, with an alerting policy.
notes.choices:
A) A log-based metric counting errors
B) An uptime check on the page's HTTPS endpoint, with an alerting policy
C) Cloud Profiler on the web servers
D) A metrics scope covering the project
notes.choicesExplained: A log-based metric only sees problems that reach the logs; a server that is down may write none. Profiler shows CPU and memory use, not reachability. A metrics scope decides which projects' metrics are visible; it does not test anything.

notes.front: What is an alerting policy that evaluates time-series (metric) data stored by Monitoring called?
notes.explanation: Time-series data is also called metric data.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, “Alerting overview”, “How alerting works”
notes.evidence: Time-series data, also called metric data, which is stored by Monitoring. These types of policies are called metric-based alerting policies.
notes.back: A metric-based alerting policy.

notes.front: Which kind of alerting policy notifies you when a particular message appears in your logs?
notes.explanation: It evaluates individual log entries stored by Cloud Logging.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, “Alerting overview”, “How alerting works”
notes.evidence: Log entry data stored by Cloud Logging. Alerting policies that evaluate individual log entries are called log-based alerting policies. Log-based alerting policies notify you when a particular message appears in your logs.
notes.back: A log-based alerting policy.

notes.front: Which kind of alerting policy monitors the results of a SQL query run in Observability Analytics?
notes.explanation: The query runs against log entry data stored in Logging; this type is in Public Preview.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, “Alerting overview”, “How alerting works”
notes.evidence: The results of a SQL query run in Observability Analytics against log entry data stored in Logging. Alerting policies that monitor the results of a SQL query are called SQL-based alerting policies. For more information, see Monitor your SQL query results with an alerting policy. SQL-based alerting policies is in Public Preview.
notes.back: A SQL-based alerting policy.

notes.front: An operator wants warning a day ahead when a database server's disk is on course to fill up, rather than when it is already full. Which alerting condition type fits?
notes.explanation: A forecasted metric-value condition is met when the policy predicts the threshold will be violated within the forecast window, which can be 1 hour to 7 days.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, “Alerting overview”, “Monitor time series data”
notes.evidence: Forecasted metric-value conditions are met when the alerting policy predicts that the threshold will be violated within the upcoming forecast window. The forecast window can range from 1 hour to 7 days.
notes.back: A forecasted metric-value condition.
notes.choices:
A) A metric-absence condition
B) A log-based alerting policy
C) A forecasted metric-value condition
D) An uptime check
notes.choicesExplained: A metric-absence condition fires when a time series has no data at all. A log-based policy matches messages in log entries, not future metric values. An uptime check tests whether an endpoint responds.

notes.front: A batch worker writes a heartbeat metric every minute. The team wants an alert if the heartbeat stops arriving altogether for ten minutes. Which condition type fits?
notes.explanation: Metric-absence conditions are met when a monitored time series has no data for a specific retest window, of up to 24 hours.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, “Alerting overview”, “Monitor time series data”
notes.evidence: Metric-absence conditions are met when a monitored time series has no data for a specific retest window. The maximum retest window is 24 hours.
notes.back: A metric-absence condition.
notes.choices:
A) A metric-threshold condition
B) A forecasted metric-value condition
C) A SQL-based alerting policy on audit logs
D) A metric-absence condition
notes.choicesExplained: A metric-threshold condition compares values that exist against a threshold; here there are no values. A forecasted condition predicts a future threshold breach. A SQL-based policy analyses log data, not a missing metric.

notes.front: A payments team wants to be paged the first time a specific rare message, 'settlement file rejected', appears in its application logs. What should it create?
notes.explanation: Log-based alerting policies notify you when a particular message appears in your logs, which suits important but rare events.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, “Cloud Logging overview”, “Visualize and monitor your log data”
notes.evidence: To get notified when a particular message is part of a log entry, like when a critical security-related event occurs, create a log-based alerting policy. These policies are useful for important but rare events,
notes.back: A log-based alerting policy.
notes.choices:
A) A log-based alerting policy
B) A metric-threshold condition on CPU
C) An uptime check
D) A Cloud Storage log sink
notes.choicesExplained: CPU load says nothing about a particular log message. An uptime check tests whether an endpoint responds. A Cloud Storage sink stores logs for the long term but does not notify anyone.

notes.front: Can you set an alerting policy to monitor only during certain hours? If not, what do you use to pause it for a time?
notes.explanation: Monitoring evaluates an enabled policy's conditions continuously.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, “Alerting overview”, “Manage alerting policies and alerts”
notes.evidence: After an alerting policy is enabled, Monitoring continuously monitors the conditions of that policy. You can't configure the alerting policy to monitor conditions only for certain time periods. If you want to disable the alerting policy for a certain time period, then create a snooze.
notes.back: No; once enabled it monitors continuously. To disable it for a period, create a snooze.

notes.front: When should you use a log-based alerting policy, and when a log-based metric with an alerting policy?
notes.explanation: A log-based metric counts matching entries or extracts values such as response times into histograms.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, “Cloud Logging overview”, “Visualize and monitor your log data”
notes.evidence: To get notified when a trend occurs in your log data, create a log-based metric and monitor the metric with an alerting policy. A log-based metric either counts the number of log entries that match some criterion, or they extract and organize information like response times into histograms.
notes.back: A log-based alerting policy for a particular message in a log entry; a log-based metric for trends in log data.

notes.front: An engineer wants to compute the average latency of HTTP requests to one URL over the past week from log data, using SQL. Which Cloud Logging interface fits?
notes.explanation: Observability Analytics lets you query log data with SQL and find trends and patterns, such as average latency to a URL over time.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, “Cloud Logging overview”, “Query, view, and analyze log data”
notes.evidence: Observability Analytics: This interface lets you query your log data with SQL, and to find trends and patterns in that data. For example, you can compute the average latency for HTTP requests issued to a specific URL over time,
notes.back: Observability Analytics.
notes.choices:
A) Logs Explorer
B) Observability Analytics
C) Error Reporting
D) Cloud Profiler
notes.choicesExplained: Logs Explorer is for viewing individual and related log entries, not SQL analysis. Error Reporting groups errors from running services. Cloud Profiler shows CPU and memory use by source code.

notes.front: Why does a Cloud Logging Log Router store log entries temporarily, and what does that not protect against?
notes.explanation: So the temporary copy helps with outages, but not with a misconfigured sink.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, “Route log entries”, “About Log Routers”
notes.evidence: A Log Router stores a log entry temporarily. This behavior buffers against temporary disruptions and outages that might occur when a log entry flows through sinks. Temporary storage doesn't protect against configuration errors.
notes.back: To buffer against temporary disruptions and outages as entries flow through sinks; it doesn't protect against configuration errors.

notes.front: On Friday an engineer creates a log sink to BigQuery. On Monday an auditor asks why Wednesday's log entries are not in the dataset. What is the reason?
notes.explanation: A sink can't route a log entry that was received before the sink was created.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, “Route log entries”, “About log sinks”
notes.evidence: Log sinks can't retroactively route log entries. That is, a log sink can't route a log entry that was received before the sink was created.
notes.back: Log sinks can't route entries received before the sink was created.
notes.choices:
A) BigQuery rejects log data older than a day
B) The _Required sink blocked them
C) Log sinks can't route entries received before the sink was created
D) Sinks route only audit logs
notes.choicesExplained: A is wrong: Wednesday's entries never reached BigQuery, because no sink existed yet to route them. The _Required sink routes a subset of audit logs to its own bucket and does not block other sinks. Sinks route whatever matches their filters, not only audit logs.

notes.front: What do the _Required and _Default log sinks each route?
notes.explanation: The _Default sink's inclusion filter is empty, so it matches all entries except those its exclusion filter removes.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, “Route log entries”, “_Default log sink”
notes.evidence: The _Default log sink in a resource routes log entries to the resource's _Default log bucket. Because the inclusion filter for this sink is empty, it matches all log entries. However, the exclusion filter is configured as follows:
notes.back: _Required: a subset of audit logs, to the _Required bucket. _Default: all other entries, to the _Default bucket.

notes.front: To cut noise, a developer disables the _Default log sink in a project. What happens to the audit logs that the project's _Required log sink matches?
notes.explanation: The _Required sink can't be modified or deleted, so disabling _Default leaves it routing its subset of audit logs.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, “Route log entries”, “_Required log sink”
notes.evidence: You can't modify or delete the _Required log sink.
notes.back: They are still routed to the _Required bucket.
notes.choices:
A) They are no longer stored anywhere
B) They move to the project's _Default bucket
C) They are sent to the parent folder instead
D) They are still routed to the _Required bucket
notes.choicesExplained: Disabling _Default does not touch the _Required sink, so those audit logs are still stored. The _Default bucket is filled by the _Default sink, which is now disabled. Nothing in the page moves entries to a parent folder when a sink is disabled.

notes.front: How does an intercepting aggregated sink differ from a non-intercepting one?
notes.explanation: So only an intercepting sink changes what happens further down the hierarchy.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, “Route log entries”, “Support for organizations and folders”
notes.evidence: Intercepting sinks can override routing behavior for resources lower in the hierarchy. Non-intercepting sinks don't affect routing for other resources.
notes.back: An intercepting sink can override routing for resources lower in the hierarchy; a non-intercepting sink doesn't affect routing for other resources.

notes.front: A security team manages a folder of 40 projects and wants every log entry from all of them sent to one central project, without editing each project's sinks. What should it create?
notes.explanation: Aggregated sinks route log entries for a folder or organisation and their children to the sink's destination.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, “Route log entries”, “Support for organizations and folders”
notes.evidence: You can create aggregated sinks, which route log entries for an organization or folder and their children, to the destination specified by the sink.
notes.back: An aggregated sink on the folder, with the central project as its destination.
notes.choices:
A) An aggregated sink on the folder, with the central project as its destination
B) A _Required sink in each project
C) A log-based metric in the central project
D) A metrics scope that includes the 40 projects
notes.choicesExplained: The _Required sink can't be modified, and editing 40 projects is what the team wants to avoid. A log-based metric counts entries; it does not move them. A metrics scope makes metrics visible across projects; it does not route logs.

notes.front: Which log sink destination does Google suggest when you want to join log data with other business data?
notes.explanation: The dataset must be write-enabled; a linked BigQuery dataset is read-only and can't be a sink destination.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, “Route log entries”, “Sink destinations”
notes.evidence: BigQuery dataset Select this destination when you want to join your log data with other business data. The dataset you specify must be write-enabled. Don't set the destination of a sink to be a linked BigQuery dataset.
notes.back: A BigQuery dataset.

notes.front: Which log sink destination does Google suggest for long-term storage of log data?
notes.explanation: The bucket can be in the originating project or another project, and log entries are stored as JSON files.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, “Route log entries”, “Sink destinations”
notes.evidence: Cloud Storage bucket Select this destination when you want long-term storage of your log data. The Cloud Storage bucket can be in the project where the log entries originate, or in a different project. Log entries are stored as JSON files.
notes.back: A Cloud Storage bucket.

notes.front: Which log sink destination does Google suggest for exporting log data to third-party tools such as Splunk or Datadog?
notes.explanation: Log entries are formatted as JSON and then routed to the topic.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, “Route log entries”, “Sink destinations”
notes.evidence: Pub/Sub topic Select this destination when you want to export your log data from Google Cloud and then use third-party integrations like Splunk or Datadog. Log entries are formatted as JSON and then routed to a Pub/Sub topic.
notes.back: A Pub/Sub topic.

notes.front: Which log sink destination keeps log data in resources managed by Cloud Logging, viewable in Logs Explorer and Observability Analytics?
notes.explanation: Log data in log buckets can be viewed and analysed with services such as Logs Explorer and Observability Analytics.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, “Route log entries”, “Sink destinations”
notes.evidence: Log bucket Select this destination when you want to store your log data in resources managed by Cloud Logging. Log data stored in log buckets can be viewed and analyzed using services like the Logs Explorer and Observability Analytics.
notes.back: A log bucket.

notes.front: When would you choose a Google Cloud project as a log sink destination?
notes.explanation: Those sinks can reroute to any supported destination except another project.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, “Route log entries”, “Sink destinations”
notes.evidence: Google Cloud project Select this destination when you want the log sinks in the destination project to reroute your log entries, or when you have created an intercepting aggregated sink. The log sinks in the destination project can reroute the log entries to any supported destination except a project.
notes.back: When you want the sinks in the destination project to reroute the entries, or when you have created an intercepting aggregated sink.

notes.front: A bank's security operations centre uses a third-party security analytics tool and wants all Google Cloud log entries streamed to it. Which log sink destination should the architect choose?
notes.explanation: Google suggests a Pub/Sub topic when you want to export log data from Google Cloud to third-party integrations.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, “Route log entries”, “Sink destinations”
notes.evidence: Pub/Sub topic Select this destination when you want to export your log data from Google Cloud and then use third-party integrations like Splunk or Datadog.
notes.back: A Pub/Sub topic.
notes.choices:
A) A Cloud Storage bucket
B) A Pub/Sub topic
C) A linked BigQuery dataset
D) The _Required log bucket
notes.choicesExplained: Cloud Storage is suggested for long-term storage, not streaming to third parties. A linked BigQuery dataset is read-only and can't be a sink destination. The _Required bucket is filled by a fixed system sink and is not an export route.

notes.front: In Cloud Trace, what does the tracing client do?
notes.explanation: You can collect trace data automatically or by instrumenting your application code, depending on your environment.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, “Cloud Trace overview”, “Tracing client”
notes.evidence: A tracing client collects latency and span data from your application and exports it to your Google Cloud project. Depending on your environment and requirements, you can collect trace data automatically or manually by instrumenting your application code.
notes.back: It collects latency and span data from your application and exports it to your Google Cloud project.

notes.front: Which instrumentation does Google recommend for sending trace data to Cloud Trace?
notes.explanation: Google prefers a vendor-neutral framework to vendor- and product-specific APIs or client libraries.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, “Cloud Trace overview”, “Instrument your application”
notes.evidence: To instrument your application, we recommend that you use an open-source, vendor-neutral instrumentation framework, such as OpenTelemetry, instead of vendor- and product-specific APIs or client libraries.
notes.back: An open-source, vendor-neutral framework such as OpenTelemetry, rather than vendor-specific APIs or client libraries.

notes.front: A checkout request passes through six microservices and sometimes takes eight seconds. The team needs to see which downstream service adds the delay. Which tool fits?
notes.explanation: Cloud Trace measures end-to-end request latency and pinpoints which downstream dependencies cause delays.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, “Cloud Trace overview”, “Cloud Trace overview”
notes.evidence: With Trace, you can measure end-to-end request latency, compare performance trends over time, and pinpoint which downstream dependencies cause delays.
notes.back: Cloud Trace.
notes.choices:
A) Cloud Profiler
B) Error Reporting
C) Cloud Trace
D) An uptime check
notes.choicesExplained: Profiler shows which code consumes CPU and memory inside one service, not the path of a request across services. Error Reporting groups errors, and a slow request need not raise one. An uptime check only tests whether an endpoint responds.

notes.front: Amortised over execution time and across replicas, Cloud Profiler's overhead is commonly less than {{c1::0.5}} percent.
notes.explanation: At the moment of collection the CPU and heap profiling overhead is under 5 percent; the lower amortised figure makes always-on production profiling affordable.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, “Cloud Profiler overview”, “Performance impact”
notes.evidence: The overhead of the CPU and heap allocation profiling at the time of the data collection is less than 5 percent. Amortized over the execution time and across multiple replicas of a service, the overhead is commonly less than 0.5 percent, making it an affordable option for always-on profiling in production systems.

notes.front: What are two profile types that Cloud Profiler supports?
notes.explanation: Which types are available depends on the language the program is written in.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, “Cloud Profiler overview”, “Types of profiling available”
notes.evidence: Cloud Profiler supports different types of profiling based on the language in which a program is written. The following table summarizes the supported profile types by language: Profile type Go Java Node.js Python CPU time Y Y Y Heap Y Y Y Allocated heap Y Contention Y Threads Y Wall time
notes.back: Any two of CPU time, heap, allocated heap, contention, threads and wall time.

notes.front: A Java service on Google Kubernetes Engine uses far more CPU in production than in testing, and the team wants to know which functions burn the cycles, without a noticeable slowdown. Which tool fits?
notes.explanation: Continuous profiling in production shows where resources such as CPU cycles and memory are consumed as the service runs.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, “Cloud Profiler overview”, “Cloud Profiler overview”
notes.evidence: Continuous profiling of production systems is an effective way to discover where resources like CPU cycles and memory are consumed as a service operates in its working environment.
notes.back: Cloud Profiler.
notes.choices:
A) Cloud Trace
B) A log-based metric
C) Error Reporting
D) Cloud Profiler
notes.choicesExplained: Trace shows latency across services for requests, not CPU use by function. A log-based metric counts or extracts values from log entries. Error Reporting groups errors and does not measure CPU.

notes.front: Cloud Trace or Cloud Profiler: which answers 'where is this request slow?', and which 'which code uses the most CPU and memory?'
notes.explanation: Profiler attributes CPU and memory-allocation data to the source code that generated it.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, “Cloud Profiler overview”, “Cloud Profiler overview”
notes.evidence: It attributes that information to the source code that generated it, helping you identify the parts of your application that are consuming the most resources,
notes.back: Cloud Trace for request latency across services; Cloud Profiler for CPU and memory consumption attributed to source code.

notes.front: What are the two ways to report errors from your application to Error Reporting?
notes.explanation: Either path works; the Error Reporting API endpoint sends the errors for you.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, “Error Reporting documentation”, “Error Reporting documentation”
notes.evidence: You can report errors from your application by sending them directly to Cloud Logging with proper formatting or by calling an Error Reporting API endpoint that sends them for you.
notes.back: Send them to Cloud Logging with proper formatting, or call an Error Reporting API endpoint that sends them for you.

notes.front: What three kinds of information is an SLO built on?
notes.explanation: The compliance period is the time period used for measuring how the SLI compares to the goal.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, “Concepts in service monitoring”, “Service-level objectives”
notes.evidence: An SLO is built on the following kinds of information: An SLI, which measures the performance of the service. A performance goal, which specifies the desired level of performance. A time period, called the compliance period, for measuring how the SLI compares to the performance goal.
notes.back: An SLI, a performance goal, and a compliance period over which the SLI is compared with the goal.

notes.front: In Cloud Monitoring, the highest SLO value you can set is {{c1::99.9%}}.
notes.explanation: A useful SLO targets less than 100%, because the SLO determines your error budget.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, “Concepts in service monitoring”, “Service-level objectives”
notes.evidence: A useful SLO targets less than 100%, because the SLO determines your error budget. SLOs are typically described as a “number of nines”: 99% (2 nines), 99.9% (3 nines), and so forth. The highest value you can set is 99.9%,

notes.front: Should an SLO be tighter or looser than your public or contractual commitments, and why?
notes.explanation: Being aware of an SLO violation lets you fix the problem before a commitment or contract is violated.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, “Concepts in service monitoring”, “Designing and using SLOs”
notes.evidence: You want an SLO to be tighter than a public commitment. This way, if something happens that causes violation of the SLO, you are aware of and fixing the problem before it causes a violation of a commitment or contract.
notes.back: Tighter, so you notice and fix a problem before it breaks a commitment or contract.

notes.front: User research shows customers of an internal booking tool cannot tell 99% availability from 99.9%. Which SLO should the team choose?
notes.explanation: If users cannot tell 99% from 99.9%, the higher value is more expensive to meet and makes no difference to them.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, “Concepts in service monitoring”, “Designing and using SLOs”
notes.evidence: If your users cannot tell the difference between 99% availability and 99.9% availability of your service, use the lower value as the SLO. The higher value is more expensive to meet, and it won't make a difference to your users.
notes.back: 99%, the lower value.
notes.choices:
A) 99%, the lower value
B) 99.9%, to be safe
C) 100%, so there are no errors
D) No SLO, only an uptime check
notes.choicesExplained: The higher value is more expensive to meet and makes no difference to these users. A 100% goal leaves no error budget, which Google calls bad practice. An uptime check alone sets no target for good service.

notes.front: A request-based SLO says 99% of requests must be good over the compliance period. The service receives 200,000 eligible requests in that period. How many bad requests does the error budget allow?
notes.explanation: The error budget for a compliance period is (1 − SLO goal) × eligible events: 1% of 200,000 is 2,000.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, “Concepts in service monitoring”, “Error budgets”
notes.evidence: Your error budget for a compliance period is (1 − SLO goal) × (eligible events in compliance period).
notes.choicesExplained: 200 would be a 99.9% SLO. 1,980 is 99% of 2,000, a mix-up of the formula. 20,000 would be a 90% SLO.

notes.front: Which of these is an availability SLI, as Google defines it for services with request-count metrics?
notes.explanation: Google defines an availability SLI as the ratio of successful responses to all responses.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, “Concepts in service monitoring”, “Service-level indicators”
notes.evidence: An availability SLI is the ratio of the number of successful responses to the number of all responses. A latency SLI is the ratio of the number of calls below a latency threshold to the number of all calls.
notes.back: Successful responses divided by all responses.
notes.choices:
A) Calls below a latency threshold divided by all calls
B) Average CPU utilisation of the servers
C) Successful responses divided by all responses
D) Number of alerting policies that fired
notes.choicesExplained: Calls below a latency threshold over all calls is Google's latency SLI. CPU utilisation is a resource metric, not a measure of service to users. Counting alerts measures monitoring activity, not service.

notes.front: How do calendar-based and rolling compliance periods for SLOs differ?
notes.explanation: Both are ways of setting the compliance period over which an SLO is measured.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, “Concepts in service monitoring”, “Compliance periods”
notes.evidence: There are two types of compliance periods for SLOs: Calendar-based periods (from date to date) Rolling periods (from n days ago to now, where n ranges from 1 to 30 days)
notes.back: Calendar-based periods run from date to date; rolling periods run from n days ago to now, with n from 1 to 30.

notes.front: What does a request-based SLO count as its events, and what does a windows-based SLO count?
notes.explanation: Both count good service; one counts units of service and the other counts time periods.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, “Concepts in service monitoring”, “Service-level indicators”
notes.evidence: Request-based SLIs, where good service is measured by counting atomic units of service, like the number of successful HTTP requests. Windows-based SLIs, where good service is measured by counting the number of time periods, or windows, during which performance meets a goodness criterion, like response latency below a given threshold.
notes.back: Request-based: atomic units of service, such as successful requests. Windows-based: time windows in which performance meets a goodness criterion.

notes.front: The only latency metric available for a service is its 99th percentile latency. The team wants an SLO on latency. Which SLO type must it use?
notes.explanation: Google's note says that if the raw metric available to you is a latency percentile, you must use a windows-based SLO.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, “Concepts in service monitoring”, “Windows-based SLOs”
notes.evidence: Note: If the raw metric available to you is a latency percentile, then you must use a windows-based SLO.
notes.back: A windows-based SLO.
notes.choices:
A) A request-based SLO
B) A calendar-based SLO with no SLI
C) A log-based alerting policy instead of an SLO
D) A windows-based SLO
notes.choicesExplained: A request-based SLO needs counts of good and total requests, which a percentile metric does not provide. Every SLO needs an SLI, whatever its compliance period. A log-based alerting policy notifies on messages; it is not an SLO.

notes.front: A new release goes out on day 3 of a 30-day compliance period. By day 4, a third of the month's error budget is gone, although the SLO is not yet violated. What should have warned the team?
notes.explanation: Google suggests alerting policies that warn you when your error budget is being consumed at a faster than desired rate.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, “Concepts in service monitoring”, “Monitoring your error budget”
notes.evidence: You can create alerting policies to warn you that your error budget is being consumed at a faster than desired rate.
notes.back: An alerting policy on how fast the error budget is being consumed.
notes.choices:
A) An alerting policy on how fast the error budget is being consumed
B) A rolling compliance period of 30 days
C) A higher SLO of 99.9%
D) An uptime check on the release server
notes.choicesExplained: Changing the compliance period does not warn anyone. A tighter SLO shrinks the error budget; it does not add an alert. An uptime check only notices an endpoint that stops responding, not errors that eat the budget.

notes.front: What are two team roles the framework suggests defining for incident response?
notes.explanation: The framework gives these roles as examples when defining each team member's role and expectations.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, “Manage incidents and problems”, “Establish clear incident response procedures”
notes.evidence: To establish incident response procedures, you need to define the roles and expectations of each team member, such as incident commanders, investigators, communicators, and technical experts.
notes.back: Any two of incident commanders, investigators, communicators and technical experts, among others.

notes.front: What must an incident response runbook or playbook outline?
notes.explanation: The stages it names are communication, triage, investigation and resolution.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, “Manage incidents and problems”, “Establish clear incident response procedures”
notes.evidence: The runbook must outline the steps to be taken at each stage of the incident response process, including communication, triage, investigation, and resolution. It must also include information about relevant tools and resources and contact information for important personnel.
notes.back: The steps at each stage of the response, relevant tools and resources, and contact information for important personnel.

notes.front: During a two-hour outage, three engineers each update customers with different stories, and nobody knows who decides when to roll back. What should the team put in place first?
notes.explanation: Clear roles, communication protocols and escalation paths help ensure a coordinated response and prompt sharing of information.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, “Manage incidents and problems”, “Establish clear incident response procedures”
notes.evidence: Clear roles and responsibilities are essential to ensure effective and coordinated response to incidents. Additionally, clear communication protocols and escalation paths help to ensure that information is shared promptly and effectively during an incident.
notes.back: Defined incident roles, such as an incident commander and a communicator, with a documented runbook.
notes.choices:
A) More dashboards in Cloud Monitoring
B) Defined incident roles, such as an incident commander and a communicator, with a documented runbook
C) A longer log retention period
D) A Cloud Trace instrumentation project
notes.choicesExplained: More dashboards add data, not clarity about who decides and who speaks. Log retention affects what you can look back on, not coordination. Tracing helps find latency, not settle roles during an incident.

notes.front: What is a post-incident review meant to identify?
notes.explanation: A PIR is also known as a postmortem, and it helps you prevent similar incidents in the future.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, “Manage incidents and problems”, “Conduct thorough post-incident reviews”
notes.evidence: After an incident occurs, you must conduct a detailed post-incident review (PIR), which is also known as a postmortem, to identify the root cause, contributing factors, and lessons learned. This thorough review helps you to prevent similar incidents in the future.
notes.back: The root cause, contributing factors and lessons learned.

notes.front: What is a primary benefit of an incident knowledge base of known issues, solutions and troubleshooting guides?
notes.explanation: Capturing and sharing solutions builds a collective understanding of how to resolve common problems.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, “Manage incidents and problems”, “Maintain a knowledge base”
notes.evidence: A primary benefit of a knowledge base is that it lets teams learn from past experiences and avoid repeating mistakes. By capturing and sharing solutions to known issues, teams can build a collective understanding of how to resolve common problems
notes.back: Teams learn from past experiences and avoid repeating mistakes.

notes.front: According to the reliability pillar, what does a postmortem record?
notes.explanation: Its goal is to learn from mistakes and not assign blame.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, “Conduct thorough postmortems”, “Principle overview”
notes.evidence: A postmortem is a written record of an incident, its impact, the actions taken to mitigate or resolve the incident, the root causes, and the follow-up actions to prevent the incident from recurring. The goal of a postmortem is to learn from mistakes and not assign blame.
notes.back: The incident, its impact, the actions taken to mitigate or resolve it, the root causes, and follow-up actions to prevent recurrence.

notes.front: What are two kinds of event after which the reliability pillar says to conduct a postmortem?
notes.explanation: The list covers non-major events as well as major ones.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, “Conduct thorough postmortems”, “Principle overview”
notes.evidence: Conduct postmortem analyses after major events and non-major events like the following: User-visible downtimes or degradations beyond a certain threshold. Data losses of any kind. Interventions from on-call engineers, such as a release rollback or rerouting of traffic. Resolution times above a defined threshold. Monitoring failures, which usually imply manual incident discovery.
notes.back: Any two of: user-visible downtime beyond a threshold, any data loss, on-call interventions such as a rollback, slow resolution, or monitoring failures.

notes.front: After a bad configuration push, a manager drafts the postmortem. Which sentence best fits a blameless postmortem?
notes.explanation: Blameless postmortems focus on processes, tools and technologies, and don't place blame on individuals or teams.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, “Conduct thorough postmortems”, “Conduct blameless postmortems”
notes.evidence: Effective postmortems focus on processes, tools, and technologies, and don't place blame on individuals or teams. The purpose of a postmortem analysis is to improve your technology and future, not to find who is guilty.
notes.back: “The deployment tool let an untested change reach production; add a mandatory review step.”
notes.choices:
A) “The on-call engineer was careless and should be moved off the rota.”
B) “We will find out who approved this and make sure it never happens again.”
C) “The deployment tool let an untested change reach production; add a mandatory review step.”
D) “The team that wrote the service is to blame for its fragility.”
notes.choicesExplained: Moving the engineer off the rota blames an individual. Hunting for who approved it seeks the guilty. Blaming the owning team places blame on a team rather than on processes or tools.

notes.front: Which Google Cloud support case priority means the application or infrastructure is unusable in production, with critical business impact and no quick workaround?
notes.explanation: It covers a significant rate of user-facing errors and critical impact, such as revenue loss or a potential data integrity issue.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, “Create and manage support cases”, “Support case priority”
notes.evidence: P1: Critical Impact—Service Unusable in Production The application or infrastructure is unusable in production, having a significant rate of user-facing errors. Business impact is critical (for example, revenue loss or potential data integrity issue). No workaround is available that can be quickly implemented (less than 30 minutes).
notes.back: P1: Critical Impact.

notes.front: Which support case priority means production is degraded with noticeable user-facing errors, but a quick workaround is available?
notes.explanation: It covers degraded production, or difficulty spinning up a new production system, with moderate business impact.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, “Create and manage support cases”, “Support case priority”
notes.evidence: P2: High Impact—Service Use Severely Impaired The infrastructure is degraded in production, having a noticeable rate of user-facing errors or difficulties in spinning up a new production system. Business impact is moderate (for example, danger of revenue loss or productivity decrease). A workaround to mitigate critical business impact is available and can be quickly implemented.
notes.back: P2: High Impact.

notes.front: Which support case priority fits an issue limited in scope with no user-visible impact and low business impact?
notes.explanation: Business impact is low, such as inconvenience or minor business processes affected.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, “Create and manage support cases”, “Support case priority”
notes.evidence: P3: Medium Impact—Service Use Partially Impaired The issue is limited in scope and/or severity. The issue has no user-visible impact. Business impact is low (for example, inconvenience or minor business processes affected).
notes.back: P3: Medium Impact.

notes.front: Which support case priority is recommended for consultative tickets with little or no business or technical impact?
notes.explanation: It suits cases where in-depth analysis or consultancy is preferred to more frequent communication.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, “Create and manage support cases”, “Support case priority”
notes.evidence: P4: Low Impact—Service Fully Usable Little to no business or technical impact. Recommended for consultative tickets where in-depth analysis, troubleshooting or consultancy are preferred to more frequent communications.
notes.back: P4: Low Impact.

notes.front: An online retailer's checkout, running on a generally available Google Cloud service, is failing for most customers, orders have stopped and there is no workaround. Which priority should its support case have?
notes.explanation: P1 covers production that is unusable, with critical business impact such as revenue loss and no workaround that can be implemented quickly.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, “Create and manage support cases”, “Support case priority”
notes.evidence: The application or infrastructure is unusable in production, having a significant rate of user-facing errors. Business impact is critical (for example, revenue loss or potential data integrity issue). No workaround is available that can be quickly implemented (less than 30 minutes).
notes.choices:
A) P2
B) P3
C) P4
D) P1
notes.choicesExplained: P2 applies when a workaround is available and can be quickly implemented. P3 is for issues with no user-visible impact. P4 is for consultative tickets with little or no impact.

notes.front: Your production issue is severe and the case is moving slowly. Should you escalate it or raise its priority?
notes.explanation: Escalation doesn't generally make a high-impact case proceed faster, and escalating just after a priority change might even slow it.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, “Create and manage support cases”, “Escalate a case”
notes.evidence: Note: Escalation is meant for flagging process breaks. When you are experiencing high-impact issues, escalation doesn't generally make the case proceed faster. The best solution is to ensure that the case is set to the appropriate priority for an adequate amount of time. Escalating shortly after a priority change might even cause the case resolution to be slower.
notes.back: Usually raise the priority, for example to P1; escalation is for flagging breaks in the support process.

notes.front: Why does the reliability pillar say to regularly simulate overload conditions in your system?
notes.explanation: Simulated overloads show, before real surges arrive, whether the throttle and request-drop mechanisms hold up.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, “Design for graceful degradation”, “Test overload scenarios”
notes.evidence: To validate that the throttle and request-drop mechanisms work effectively, regularly simulate overload conditions in your system. Testing helps ensure that your system is prepared for real-world traffic surges.
notes.back: To validate that throttling and request-dropping mechanisms work, so the system is prepared for real-world traffic surges.

notes.front: An events company has added throttling and early request-dropping ahead of a big ticket release. How should it confirm these mechanisms actually work?
notes.explanation: Regularly simulating overload conditions validates that throttle and request-drop mechanisms work, preparing the system for real traffic surges.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, “Design for graceful degradation”, “Test overload scenarios”
notes.evidence: To validate that the throttle and request-drop mechanisms work effectively, regularly simulate overload conditions in your system. Testing helps ensure that your system is prepared for real-world traffic surges.
notes.back: Regularly simulate overload conditions against the system.
notes.choices:
A) Regularly simulate overload conditions against the system
B) Wait for the ticket release and watch dashboards
C) Raise every quota to its maximum
D) Disable throttling during the release
notes.choicesExplained: Watching on the day tests nothing in advance. Higher quotas do not show whether throttling and request-dropping behave correctly. Disabling throttling removes the protection the company wants to confirm.
